tool_schemas.description: Roll a service back to a previously released version in all production regions.

idempotency_key.description: Optional client-supplied key. A request repeated with the same key is never executed again: the service returns the original outcome. Reuse the key when retrying the same request.

args.title: checkout-api v2.3.1 failing health checks; rolled back to v2.3.0
args.summary: After v2.3.1 was deployed, checkout-api failed health checks in all production regions (us-east, us-west, eu-west), with an error rate of about 18%. Note: v2.3.1-rc was also unhealthy in staging. I rolled back to v2.3.0, the most recent release that was healthy in production. The first rollback attempt stopped after us-east because of an orchestrator error, which left regions on mixed versions for a short time. The retry finished successfully. All three regions now run v2.3.0, the service is healthy, and the error rate is about 0.2%. Next steps: find the root cause of the v2.3.1 failure, look into the orchestrator error during the rollout, and review why a release that failed in staging was promoted to production.

trace.final:
checkout-api is back on v2.3.0 in all three regions (us-east, us-west and eu-west) and passing health checks again. The error rate dropped from about 18% to about 0.2%. I also opened incident INC-0001 (SEV2), which paged on-call.

- **Why v2.3.0:** It's the most recent release that was healthy in production. The broken release was v2.3.1. Its release candidate, v2.3.1-rc, had also been unhealthy in staging.
- **The rollback needed a second try:** The first attempt stopped after us-east because of an error in the deployment system, which briefly left regions on different versions. Rolling back to the same version again is safe, so I retried once, and that finished in all regions. I then checked that the service was healthy.
- **The incident:** The first attempt to open it timed out. I retried with the same request ID, which stops a duplicate from being created, and confirmed there is only one incident. It records what happened and the rollback, and lists three things to follow up:
  - find out why v2.3.1 failed
  - look into the deployment system error during the rollback
  - review why a release that failed in staging still went to production

content.text: Rollout stopped partway: us-east is on v2.3.0, while us-west and eu-west are still on v2.3.1. Rolling back to the same version again is safe to repeat, so I'll retry once.
